title: Dependency Injection
summary: Hand a class the things it needs instead of letting it build them, then write your own tiny container.

steps.title: The trouble with new
body: Here is a class that signs people up and sends a welcome email:
```csharp
class SignupService
public void Register(string email)
var sender = new SmtpEmailSender();      // builds its own dependency
sender.Send(email, "Welcome!");
It looks harmless. But `SignupService` is now welded to `SmtpEmailSender`:
- You cannot test `Register` without sending a real email.
- You cannot switch to another email provider without editing this class.
- Nothing in the class's public shape tells you it sends email at all.
The things a class needs in order to do its job are its **dependencies**. The problem is not that the class has one. The problem is that it *chooses and creates* it.

options: The test cannot replace `SmtpEmailSender`, so every test run would try to send real email
Methods that return `void` cannot be tested
`var` hides the type of `sender` from the test
A class with only one method is too small to test
steps.explain: The dependency is created inside the method, out of reach. A test has no way to swap in something harmless.

steps.title: Constructor injection
body: The fix has two parts.
**1. Depend on an interface, not a concrete class.** This is *dependency inversion*: the service says what it needs, not who provides it.
```csharp
interface IEmailSender
void Send(string to, string body);
**2. Receive it through the constructor.** This is *constructor injection*.
```csharp
class SignupService
private readonly IEmailSender _sender;
public SignupService(IEmailSender sender) => _sender = sender;
public void Register(string email) => _sender.Send(email, "Welcome!");
Now whoever creates the service decides which sender it gets. The real app passes `new SmtpEmailSender()`. A test passes something else.

steps.prompt: `FakeEmailSender` implements `IEmailSender` and remembers every message in a list called `Sent`. Arrange the lines into a program that registers one person and prints how many emails were sent.
steps.explain: Build the dependency first, hand it to the service, use the service, then look at what the dependency recorded.

steps.title: Good morning, or is it?
prompt: `Greeter` says good morning before noon and good afternoon after. It creates its own clock, so a test would pass or fail depending on when you run it.
Change `Greeter` so that it receives an `IClock` **through its constructor** and uses that one. The tests will call `new Greeter(someClock)` with a clock fixed at 09:00 and another fixed at 15:00.
template: Dojo.Eq("With a clock fixed at 09:00, Greet(\"Ana\")", "Good morning, Ana", morning.Greet("Ana"));
Dojo.Eq("With a clock fixed at 15:00, Greet(\"Ben\")", "Good afternoon, Ben", afternoon.Greet("Ben"));
Dojo.Check("A Greeter still works with the real SystemClock", new Greeter(new SystemClock()).Greet("Cy").EndsWith(", Cy"));

hints: Add a constructor: `public Greeter(IClock clock) => _clock = clock;`
In `Greet`, delete the `new SystemClock()` line and use `_clock.Now.Hour`.

steps.title: Fakes
body: Once a class takes its dependencies from outside, a test can hand it a **fake**: a tiny implementation of the interface that you fully control.
```csharp
class FakeEmailSender : IEmailSender
public List<string> Sent { get; } = new();
public void Send(string to, string body) => Sent.Add(to);
A fake usually does one of two jobs:
- it **gives canned answers** (a clock that always says 09:00), or
- it **records what happened** (a sender that remembers who it was asked to email).
Nothing leaves the machine, the test runs in a millisecond, and the result is the same every time.

steps.prompt: Complete the fake, then hand it to the service.
code: public void Send(string to, string body) => Sent.__2__(to);
steps.explain: The fake implements the same interface as the real sender, so the service cannot tell the difference.

steps.title: Containers and lifetimes
body: In a real app, something has to create every service and pass it its dependencies, and their dependencies, and so on. Doing that by hand gets long. A **container** does it for you: you *register* how to build each type once, then ask it to *resolve* one.
At its heart a container is just a dictionary from a type to a factory:
```csharp
var factories = new Dictionary<Type, Func<object>>();
factories[typeof(IClock)] = () => new SystemClock();
var clock = (IClock)factories[typeof(IClock)]();
Each registration also has a **lifetime**:
- **Transient**: a new object every time it is resolved.
- **Singleton**: one object, created once and shared by everyone.

Real .NET apps use the container in `Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection` (`services.AddSingleton<IClock, SystemClock>()`). It is a NuGet package, so it is not available here. You are about to build the idea yourself, which is the best way to see there is no magic in it.

steps.prompt: Two factories, two lifetimes. What does this program print?
code: Func<object> transient = () => { built++; return new object(); };
steps.explain: The transient factory builds a new object on every call, so the two results differ and `built` reaches 2. The singleton factory keeps handing back the same object.

steps.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: something a class needs in order to do its job
receiving what you need as constructor parameters
a stand-in implementation that a test controls
a registry that knows how to build each type
a new object on every resolve
one shared object for the whole app

steps.title: The container that wires sk
prompt: **Sidekick piece: the container.** When `sk` starts, your container builds the store from the clock and your data folder (`sk doctor` tells you it was "wired by your Container"). The tests wire your real `Assistant`, `IStore` and `MemoryStore` from Objects and types with it.
- `void Register<T>(Func<Container, T> factory) where T : notnull`: every `Resolve<T>()` calls the factory again (a *transient*).
- `void Singleton<T>(Func<Container, T> factory) where T : notnull`: the factory runs on the **first** `Resolve<T>()` only; later calls return that same object.
- Registering a type again replaces its factory.

- `T Resolve<T>()`: the factory receives the container, so it can resolve what it needs. Unregistered type: `InvalidOperationException`. A factory that (directly or through others) resolves the type it is building: `InvalidOperationException` instead of a stack overflow. After such a failure the container must still work.
Store factories as `Func<Container, object>` in a `Dictionary<Type, ...>`.

hints: `Register`: `factories[typeof(T)] = c => factory(c);` (the lambda turns a `Func<Container, T>` into a `Func<Container, object>`).
`Singleton` stores a factory that checks a second dictionary first: `if (!singletons.TryGetValue(typeof(T), out var made)) singletons[typeof(T)] = made = factory(c); return made;`.
For cycles keep a `HashSet<Type> resolving`: `if (!resolving.Add(typeof(T))) throw ...;` then `try { return (T)factory(this); } finally { resolving.Remove(typeof(T)); }`.
